flashcards.q: What are the four core XOR identities the whole pattern rests on?
Every element appears twice except one — how do you find it, and in what time/space?
flashcards.a: XOR-reduce the whole array; O(n) time, O(1) space.

flashcards.q: Why does plain XOR-reduce fail when every element appears three times except one?
flashcards.a: x^x^x = x, not 0 — triples don't cancel. Need per-bit counting mod 3 instead.

flashcards.q: Two elements appear once, rest appear twice. What's the recovery trick after XOR-reducing to get x^y?
flashcards.a: Isolate the lowest set bit of x^y via v & -v, use it to partition the array into two buckets, XOR-reduce each bucket separately.

flashcards.q: How do you build a prefix-XOR array and answer range-XOR queries?
flashcards.a: pre[i+1] = pre[i] ^ a[i]; xor(l,r) = pre[r+1] ^ pre[l], same mechanism as prefix sums.

flashcards.q: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array — what data structure and approach?
flashcards.a: Bitwise trie built MSB to LSB; for each number greedily walk toward the opposite bit at each level. O(32n).

flashcards.q: Why does v & -v isolate the lowest set bit of v?
flashcards.a: Two's complement: -v = ~v+1 flips all bits below the lowest set bit to 0 and inverts the rest, so ANDing with v leaves only that one bit.

flashcards.q: What Python-specific bug bites Single Number II implementations?
flashcards.a: Python ints are unbounded, so a 32-bit bit-counting result must be manually reinterpreted as signed (subtract 2^32 if >= 2^31); Java/Go don't need this since their ints are already fixed-width.
